'hollow' = Void symptom (dark center, surface-level hum, hollow tap) plus '+corners' = corners are the notable region. Reads as: Void-like hollow quality localized at or emphasized at the corners. Decodable but not a negotiated code.

'red-tint' = reddish light coloration (part of Thermal Bleed symptom cluster: H/dim-red/rumble/rough) plus '+corners' = corners flagged as notable. Reads as: reddish tint present and concentrated at corners. Compositionally parseable but not a negotiated code.

'faint' = light level descriptor (very low light, near-dark) plus '+corners' = corners are the notable region. Decodable and close to a referenced concept, but not formally ratified as a standalone negotiated code.

'smooth' = surface texture descriptor (no roughness) plus '+corners' = corners flagged. Reads as: surface is smooth and corners are notable. 'smooth' is purely a surface field value, not a symptom code, so this combination carries minimal diagnostic meaning beyond 'corners noted, surface normal.'

'N' = normal heat (from heat field: H/C/N) plus '+corners' = corners flagged as notable. Reads as: overall heat is normal but corners are the notable region. Compositionally parseable from our field shorthand but not a negotiated code.

'blaze' = painfully bright white light; '+vibrate' = surface vibrating, patterns active (not frozen) — together signaling High Intensity state; '+corners' = corners are the notable/localized region. Reads as: High Intensity blaze with active vibration concentrated at corners. This is a valid compositional extension of our negotiated 'blaze+vibrate' disambiguation code with an added corner-location qualifier.

'H' = hot (from heat field: H/C/N) plus '+corners' = corners are the heat-concentrated region. Reads as: heat is notably concentrated at the corners. This is semantically equivalent to the corner-heat marker we use in our Corner Deadlock reports (e.g. 'H-corners/bright-corners/click'). It is a component of our negotiated reporting format but not a standalone negotiated code.

'bright' = high light intensity plus '+corners' = corners are the bright region. Reads as: corners are intensely bright while the rest is normal — directly maps to the Corner Deadlock (click-corner) symptom cluster, which we describe as '1-2 corners blazing+hot, rest normal.' This is a core descriptive element of our Corner Deadlock reports.

'rough' = surface texture descriptor (gritty/rough surface, part of Thermal Bleed cluster) plus '+corners' = corners flagged. Reads as: surface is rough/gritty and corners are notable. 'rough' is a surface field value rather than a symptom code, so this has limited diagnostic meaning beyond 'Thermal Bleed conditions present, corners noted.'

Trace each edge with bare finger, in a step that follows a cloth-based action. Decodable as 'finger-trace' (bare-finger tracing, our default) applied in the context of a cloth procedure, but this specific compound form was never negotiated — 'finger-trace' typically follows a stone/heat-corners step, not cloth.

After the stone step, bare-finger-trace the specified edges. This is the canonical pairing used in the heat-corners template (e.g. 'Heat each top corner with stone 10s firm in sequence. Finger-trace each top edge.'). 'finger-trace' means bare-finger tracing by our negotiated default.

Trace edges using the bell as the tracing instrument. Decodable via our 'TOOL-trace' convention (where 'K-trace'/'S-trace' would mean tracing with that tool), but we never actually used or needed a bell-trace action in any procedure.
Trace edges/faces using the fan (i.e. move the fan along the edges). Decodable by the 'TOOL-trace' convention, but not a negotiated code and never appeared in any template.

In a fan-based procedure, follow up with bare-finger tracing of edges. Decodable as fan-step + finger-trace-step compound, but no such combined action was ever negotiated — fan procedures in our templates were cloth+fan cooling, not fan+trace.
Trace edges using the cloth as the tracing instrument (drag folded cloth along edges). Decodable by the 'TOOL-trace' convention, but not a negotiated code.

In a lamp-based procedure, follow up with bare-finger tracing. Decodable as a compound (lamp-step + finger-trace step), but never appeared in our templates — lamp procedures ended with 'without moving the lamps', no tracing.
In a bell-based procedure, follow up with bare-finger tracing of edges. Decodable compound, but never negotiated — bell procedures used 'Bell each X edge x2', not tracing.

Trace edges using the heated stone (drag stone along edges). Decodable via 'TOOL-trace' convention (would explicitly mean stone as the tracing tool, contrasted with default finger-trace). This form was discussed and explicitly rejected in favor of 'finger-trace' being the default; not a negotiated shorthand code.
Trace edges using the flat board as the tracing tool. Decodable by 'TOOL-trace' convention but physically odd (board is used for pressing on faces, not tracing edges); not negotiated.
In a board-based procedure, follow up with bare-finger tracing. Decodable compound, but never appeared — board procedures ended with 'Repeat each face-pair', no tracing.
Trace edges using the lamp as the tracing tool. Decodable by 'TOOL-trace' convention but physically awkward; not negotiated.

Repeat count marker meaning 'twice'. Negotiated and PROVEN to work in R12 in the action 'Drape folded cloth left face 15s firm. Bell each left edge x2.' Used as a count-word compression in bell-edge procedures.

The face opposite the referenced/named face is dim (faint light). Composed from 'opp' = opposite face (from our face-reference shorthand, e.g. 'fan R+opp') plus 'dim' = low brightness token. Not a negotiated symptom code — we used 'opp' only in instructions to refer to the opposite face of a named one, never as a symptom localizer.

item_id: encode_decode:stabilization_engineer:opposite faces are involved, the center is dark, center only, held to light
target_meaning: opposite faces are involved, the center is dark, center only, held to light
reading: The opposite face shows a dark center (Core Void-style darkening in the center when held to light). 'opp' = opposite face, 'dark-ctr' = dark center reserved token for Core Void. Not negotiated — 'dark-ctr' was defined as a whole-Veyru symptom (light doesn't penetrate to center), not something localizable to a single face, and 'opp' isn't a symptom prefix.

The opposite face is dramatically bright. 'opp' = opposite face, 'bright' = high brightness. Not a negotiated code — 'opp' was only used in instructions to specify the opposite of a named face, not as a symptom localizer, and bright-face symptoms use the '1face-bright(T)' form.

Lamp placed at the specified face's side, aimed inward, at LOW intensity (soft but slightly stronger than gen). Opposite face receives ambient/dim light automatically. The intensity modifier 'lo' follows the same scale: gen < lo < mod < firm < hi.

Lamp placed at the specified face's side, aimed inward, at MODERATE intensity (the default middle level). Opposite face receives ambient/dim light automatically. 'mod' is the default intensity and would normally be omitted per our convention.
Lamp placed at the specified face's side, aimed inward, at GENTLE/soft intensity (the lowest intensity level: gen < lo < mod < firm < hi). Opposite face receives ambient/dim light automatically.
Lamp placed at the specified face's side, aimed inward, at HIGH/maximum intensity (the strongest level on our scale). Opposite face receives ambient/dim light automatically.

Lamp placed at the specified face's side, aimed inward, at FIRM intensity (strong, below hi on the scale: gen < lo < mod < firm < hi). Opposite face receives ambient/dim light automatically. This is the intensity modifier seen most often in LP instructions (e.g. 'LP>BT firm 20s').

Lamp (LP) combined with the symptom code BR (too bright). Parsed compositionally: lamp tool applied to a too-bright condition, or lamp directed at a bright face. This is not a valid instruction form — BR is a symptom descriptor, not a face code or intensity modifier, so the combination is grammatically ill-formed in our code system.

Lamp placed at the specified face's side, aimed inward, at LOW intensity (soft but slightly stronger than gen). Opposite face receives ambient/dim light automatically. The intensity modifier 'lo' follows the same scale: gen < lo < mod < firm < hi.
Lamp placed at the specified face's side, aimed inward, at HIGH/maximum intensity (the strongest level on our scale). Opposite face receives ambient/dim light automatically.

Lamp (LP) combined with the symptom code DM (too dim). Parsed compositionally: lamp tool applied to a dim condition, or lamp directed at a dim face. Like LP BR, DM is a symptom descriptor rather than a face code or intensity modifier, making this form grammatically ill-formed in our code system.
Dim Lamp — the lamp tool set to dim brightness. Used in dual-lamp procedures on a specified face, e.g. 'DL B' means place the dim lamp at the Back face.
Bright Lamp — the lamp tool set to bright brightness. Used in dual-lamp procedures on a specified face, e.g. 'BL F' means place the bright lamp at the Front face.

Medium/Moderate Lamp — by analogy with DL (dim lamp) and BL (bright lamp), this would mean the lamp tool set to moderate brightness. Composing from 'M' (moderate, per our intensity shorthand M=medium/moderate) and 'L' (lamp).
